comparison: Perfect agreement on CETSA data showing heliomycin and 4-dmH binding to SIRT1 (C8-C9, C47-C54). Both evaluations find the thermal stabilization data with specific OC50 values and TM increases strongly support the biophysical interaction claims.

Complete agreement on apoptosis induction by 4-dmH in HSC-3 cells (C13, C65, C72-C77). Both evaluations accept the JC-1 staining, western blot data showing pro-apoptotic markers, and p53-independence of the apoptotic pathway.

Strong agreement on in vivo efficacy (C17-C20, C118-C122, C125-C127). Both evaluations accept the tumor volume reduction data and western blot analysis from tumor tissues showing 4-dmH superiority over heliomycin.

Complete agreement on autophagy induction by heliomycin in Ca9-22 cells (C14, C62-C64, C67-C71). Both evaluations accept the AO staining, lack of JC-1 staining, and autophagy marker upregulation as supporting the differential cell death pathway.

Strong agreement on main conclusions (C21, C134, C141, C155-C157). Both evaluations accept the overall mechanistic model linking differential target binding to therapeutic outcomes, with peer reviewers explicitly affirming the mechanistic explanation.

Complete agreement on SIRT1 degradation mechanism (C57-C61). Both evaluations accept the western blots, MG132 rescue experiments, and immunoprecipitation data showing ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated degradation.

Complete agreement on selective cytotoxicity and anti-proliferative effects (C78-C81, C83). Both evaluations accept the cell impedance, colony formation, and cell cycle data without raising concerns about selectivity or mechanism.

Strong agreement on differential binding specificity (C10, C45, C95-C98, C102). Both evaluations accept that 4-dmH binds tNOX while heliomycin does not, based on CETSA data. This is identified as a key finding by both peer reviewers.

Complete agreement on tNOX degradation mechanism (C89-C93). Both evaluations accept the ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation pathway for tNOX, with peer reviewers explicitly confirming p53-independence.

Agreement on molecular docking predictions for tNOX binding (C110-C117). Both evaluations accept the computational data as supporting the experimental CETSA findings, with peer reviewers explicitly mentioning in silico docking as valid supporting evidence.

Divergent evaluation of patient sample data (C15-C16, C128). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to small sample size (n=5), while peer reviewers accept the finding without questioning statistical power. Both accept the TCGA survival analysis (C129-C131).

Agreement on SIRT1 docking simulations (C103-C108). Both evaluations accept the computational predictions, though OpenEval notes the interpretation about H-bond effects (C108) is speculative. Peer reviewers do not raise this concern.

Agreement on clinical relevance from TCGA analysis (C129-C133). Both evaluations accept the Kaplan-Meier survival data showing tNOX correlation with poor prognosis in stage-III patients, supporting therapeutic rationale.
Agreement on target specificity controls (C99-C101). Both evaluations accept the negative CETSA results for PARP and NOX4, supporting the specificity of 4-dmH for tNOX and SIRT1.
Agreement on in vitro SIRT1 inhibition (C55-C56). Both evaluations accept the biochemical activity assays showing SIRT1 inhibition by both compounds, with no concerns raised about the data.
Agreement on SIRT1 biology background (C86-C87). Both evaluations accept the established knowledge about SIRT1's role in NAD+ metabolism as valid context for the experimental findings.
Agreement on NAD+/NADH ratio changes (C11, C85). Both evaluations accept the metabolic data linking tNOX inhibition to NAD+ metabolism, supporting the mechanistic model.
Agreement on tNOX knockdown validation (C94). Both evaluations accept the siRNA experiments as supporting the functional role of tNOX in the proposed mechanism.
Agreement on computational predictions (C139-C140). Both evaluations accept the convergence of docking simulations with experimental data as supporting the mechanistic conclusions.
